Chloroplast. These are the large, membrane-bound organelles that you find in plant and algal cells, and they're the engine of photosynthesis. They convert light energy into chemical energy by using the green pigment chlorophyll. Inside chloroplasts, you've got stacked membrane structures called thylakoids where the light reactions happen, and then a fluid-filled inner compartment called the stroma where the Calvin cycle fixes carbon dioxide. Like mitochondria, chloroplasts carry their own DNA and ribosomes—a telltale sign of their ancestry as free-living bacteria.

The structure is carefully organized. There's a double-membrane envelope enclosing the stroma. The thylakoid membranes arrange themselves into stacks called grana, which is where light capture occurs. The stroma houses the enzymes of the Calvin cycle and also stores starch granules. Chlorophyll sits embedded in those thylakoid membranes and absorbs the light energy. Within the thylakoids are protein complexes called Photosystem I and Photosystem II—these split water molecules, generate ATP, and produce NADPH, all powered by light.

The chloroplast's own DNA encodes essential photosynthetic proteins, and it maintains prokaryotic-like ribosomes that allow it to make some of its own proteins. This chloroplast evolved through endosymbiosis—billions of years ago, early eukaryotic cells engulfed cyanobacteria, and over time this became a permanent partnership.

Chloroplast dysfunction directly affects crop yields and plays a crucial role in how plants respond to environmental stress like drought and temperature extremes.
